name: Connecticut
summary_text: Connecticut is a state within the United States, and its laws stand under the national framework that governs a trans visitor's entry, identity documents and screening. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.  Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs. Screening at checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Visa applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex can be treated as committing fraud and barred permanently, and since February 2025 trans athletes have been barred from entering the country to compete in women's sports, with an internal marking applied to flagged applicants.  Care access for a visitor is constrained at the federal layer. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.  Against that national backdrop, Connecticut's own law runs in the opposite direction. A July 2026 national legal-risk ranking, built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver-licence restrictions and the end of legal recognition, places Connecticut in a fifteen-state most-protective tier whose laws have gone above and beyond in safeguarding trans rights.  Connecticut also operates a shield or refuge law. The MAP Transgender Healthcare Equality Map, with data as of 27 September 2026, lists Connecticut as a state holding a shield law or executive order dating from 2022. The shield protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges where the care is legal in Connecticut but banned in the person's home state, which makes the state directly relevant to a visitor travelling from a state with a youth-care ban.

name: Delaware
summary_text: Delaware is a state within the United States, and the rules that govern entry, travel documents and identity screening are federal in every respect. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker; new passport applications are decided as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU is litigating on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and in November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.  Visa screening carries its own exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 and the State Department announcement of 25 February 2025 refuse visas to transgender people seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events, flag such applicants with an internal marking, and treat listing a gender other than the sex assigned at birth as grounds for a permanent ban on grounds of fraud.  Screening at United States checkpoints carries an outing risk. TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments have responded to these rules: in April 2025 CNN reported advisories issued about transgender people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.  The federal facility restriction reaches Delaware directly. Executive Order 14168 bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, which covers federal buildings a visitor may enter. Nationally, a Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to transgender people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, and some states making trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law. Delaware records no such ban.  On state-level posture, a July 2026 national legal risk assessment lists Delaware within its Low-Risk States group, alongside Arizona, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Virginia, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia. The assessment characterises these jurisdictions as largely refraining from targeting transgender adults, while noting that none of them specialises in protecting them. Delaware's position therefore reflects the absence of state-level targeting rather than the presence of state-level protection, and it does not insulate a visitor from the federal measures above.  Federal health-care restrictions apply nationwide. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
